item.title: US stocks: Nasdaq ends down as chipmakers fall and bank earnings roll in
item.description: In a recent trading session, the Nasdaq index took a hit as chip stocks continued their downward spiral, amid diverging results from major banks like Citigroup and Goldman Sachs. The PHLX chip index faced a substantial decline, sparking fears surrounding competition in this sector. Despite the turbulence, analysts express optimism about future earnings linked to AI-driven innovations.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: The Nasdaq ended lower on Tuesday, as chip stocks added to recent losses and investors parsed mixed quarterly results from Citigroup and other big US banks.The PHLX chip index fell for a fifth straight session, after Broadcom CEO Hock Tan on Monday likened some of the investment flow into the sector to casino gambling. Additionally, reports of technological advances by Chinese memory chip company CXMT underscored concerns about rising competition.Micron Technology and Applied Materials both fell sharply. Broadcom rose.Citigroup dipped and Goldman Sachs rose after both banks topped profit estimates.Wells Fargo fell after its net interest income missed estimates, while JPMorgan Chase swung between gains and losses following a rare profit miss.Apple hit an intraday record high.Analysts on average see S&P 500 third-quarter earnings surging over 30%, fueled largely by AI-related technology companies, according to LSEG data.Expectations of a strong earnings season have offset worries about the US war with Iran, surging bond yields and inflation related to high oil prices.Also Read | NY Fed President Williams sees no need for a rate hike in 2027 A lot of investors are feeling a sense of relief that markets might start looking at earnings and less at the bond market, less at higher-for-longer oil prices and less at high interest rates, said Jake Dollarhide, CEO of Longbow Asset Management in Tulsa, Oklahoma.According to preliminary data, the S&P 500 lost 1.41 points, or 0.02%, to end at 7,805.83 points, while the Nasdaq Composite lost 42.37 points, or 0.15%, to 27,203.53. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 173.10 points, or 0.33%, to 51,677.45.The S&P 500 has rallied about 14% in 2026, lifted by AI-related technology stocks. However, the median stock in the index is up less than 5% and over 200 S&P 500 components are down for the year.Reflecting expectations of strong corporate earnings from AI heavyweights, the S&P 500 is trading at under 19 times expected earnings, its lowest since 2023.The PHLX chip index has lost more than 8% in the past five sessions and it remains up over 70% year-to-date.The S&P 500 healthcare index fell on Tuesday, with Johnson & Johnson down despite topping profit estimates.Bumble jumped after the dating-app operator agreed to go private in a $1.3 billion deal.Domino's Pizza declined after scaling back its full-year sales outlook.

item.title: NY Fed President Williams sees no need for a rate hike in 2027
item.description: At a recent conference, John Williams from the Federal Reserve Bank of New York expressed optimism about a potential interest-rate increase this year, suggesting inflation could hit the 2% goal by next year. He cited the role of artificial intelligence in affecting inflation rates while also addressing the sector's supply-demand imbalance.
item.dc:creator: Bloomberg
item.content:encoded: Federal Reserve Bank of New York President John Williams said he still sees one more interest-rate hike as appropriate this year, but at the moment doesn’t believe it will be necessary for the central bank to increase rates again in 2027.“I haven’t changed my view that it may be appropriate to have one more rate hike,” Williams said Tuesday in an interview with Bloomberg News at the New York Fed. “I don’t think at this time I have any reason to believe that we would need to do more” after that.Williams said there are still signs inflation will slow “quite a bit” and approach the Fed’s 2% target next year, as the impacts from tariffs and an energy price shock fade. That, along with other signs that underlying inflation is cooling, should help overcome the price pressures driven by the build-out of infrastructure for artificial intelligence, he said.US Treasury yields edged lower after Williams’ remarks, with those on two-year notes — most sensitive to the Fed’s rate path — erasing an increase of as much as three basis points.Williams’ remarks put him in line with the median of rate projections released by Fed officials after they agreed to raise rates by a quarter percentage point at their September gathering. A number of his colleagues, however — including Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack and Dallas’ Lorie Logan — have made clear they believe more than one additional move will be required to bring inflation back to 2%.Investors currently anticipate the Fed will raise rates in December and twice more in 2027, based on pricing in federal funds futures.The New York Fed chief emphasized the high level of uncertainty around his outlook and, in particular, said he continues to watch the AI component of inflation closely.Also Read | US chip stocks slide as China’s CXMT advances; AI spending fears rattle investors“It’s still mid-October,” he said. “This economy is being affected by lots of different influences, and we just have to keep watching the data.”Policymakers will get a fresh report on consumer price inflation on Wednesday, the last one before they meet on Oct. 27-28.September ShiftWilliams wasn’t among policymakers calling forcefully for a rate increase in the run-up to the September move. But, he said, he “firmly supported” the September increase after two factors altered the short-term inflation outlook.First, earlier expectations that the Iran conflict might get resolved and oil prices would fall proved overly optimistic. In addition, the spread between oil prices and the prices for refined products increased markedly in recent months. “We’ve seen, I think, an additional shock, if you will, or additional manifestation of these developments in terms of much higher fuel costs,” he said.But that hasn’t altered his longer-term outlook for prices.“I still believe there’s disinflationary forces at play,” he said. “We definitely had the effects of tariffs and the energy prices, and now with AI. But some of those are, I think, not indicating upward movement in underlying inflation. In fact, these measures of underlying inflation have come down.”Importantly, he added, there’s no sign that the labor market is out of balance and contributing to inflation.“This is not an economy that is overheating overall,” he said. “This is not an economy where this added inflationary pressure is beyond these particular shocks that we’re experiencing.”Still, Williams acknowledged that demand related to the AI build-out was outpacing supply, and that mismatch wouldn’t be resolved for some time.“It is an unusual circumstance that we have one sub-sector of the economy that seems to be running at all cylinders and is going to keep going for a while,” he said. “But I think it’s really about looking at the broader economy.”He also remained optimistic that AI will eventually deliver productivity gains that will be disinflationary. Predicting when that might happen, however, is extremely difficult, he said.Forward GuidanceWilliams also spoke about a speech he delivered on Sept. 29 that proved crucial in reining in market expectations for another rate increase this month. In those remarks, Williams said there was little urgency for the Fed to hike again in the wake of the September move. His comments were followed by similar remarks from Vice Chair Philip Jefferson. Many Fed watchers speculated that the speeches were coordinated, possibly with Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh, to prevent a surprise for investors.On Tuesday, Williams said market pricing was “useful information,” but his speech reflected only his own views.“In September we had two months of data. It was an opportunity to assess, evaluate what are the underlying trends telling us,” he said.The president of the New York Fed holds a permanent vote on monetary policy decisions and acts as vice chair of the Federal Open Market Committee. Together with the chair and vice chair of the Fed’s Board of Governors, the New York Fed chief is traditionally considered part of the central bank’s leadership “troika.”“I’m in regular contact with the chairman,” Williams said. “We meet frequently, but I’m not going to say anything more about that.”

item.title: US chip stocks slide as China’s CXMT advances; AI spending fears rattle investors
item.description: Shares in US chip manufacturers tumbled, primarily influenced by memory and data storage firms, following competitive moves from China's CXMT. The sector faced significant pressure, stemming from concerns over escalating rivalry and demands for AI investments. Key players like Micron Technology, Seagate Technology, SanDisk, and Western Digital saw notable declines in their stock prices.
item.dc:creator: ETMarkets.com
item.content:encoded: US chip stocks fell on Tuesday, led by memory-chip and data-storage companies, after reports of a technological advance by China’s CXMT raised concerns about intensifying competition. Questions about heavy artificial-intelligence spending added to pressure on a sector that has rallied sharply this year, Reuters reported.The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index dropped 1.5%, extending its decline to a fifth consecutive session and touching its lowest level in about four weeks.Micron Technology fell 4.5% to its lowest level since September 16, marking its fourth straight daily decline. Data-storage companies also suffered steep losses, with SanDisk down 4.3%, Seagate Technology falling 5.9% and Western Digital sliding 5.8%.According to the Reuters report, Chinese memory-chip maker CXMT has made “key progress” on a new cell architecture designed to increase memory density. South Korea’s Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix are working on similar technology.Samsung shares tumbled more than 7% in South Korea, while SK Hynix dropped over 10%.Robert Pavlik, senior portfolio manager at Dakota Wealth, described the selloff as a rush to lock in profits as investors reassess the threat of greater competition.Concerns about AI investment also weighed on the sector after Broadcom CEO Hock Tan compared such spending to “casino gambling.” Broadcom shares slipped 0.3%.Elsewhere, Nvidia declined 0.4%, Intel fell 1.1%, AMD lost 1.2%, and Marvell Technology dropped 2.2%.Despite its recent losses, the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index remains up more than 70% this year, supported by expectations of strong AI-related demand.(Disclaimer: This article is based on inputs from agencies. These do not represent the views of The Economic Times)
